name: Atwood Commons
award: 2025 Federal 4% and state housing tax credits (Round Two)
headline: Brikwell's Atwood Commons is a planned four-story, 72-unit building for households earning 30% to 80% AMI at 130 Third Avenue in downtown Longmont, across from the OUR Center. It won 2025 Round Two federal 4% and state housing tax credits from CHFA, with $14.25M of tax-exempt bonds.
why_it_matters: It shows how fragile voucher-backed underwriting has become: eight committed project-based vouchers were withdrawn in February 2026 after HUD budget talks, and the City of Longmont filled the $1.4M gap with a 100% fee waiver and a larger Affordable Housing Fund loan so the deal could close in summer 2026.

status.label: Bonds authorized; closing set for 2026-08-10 but not confirmed by a dated public record
status.detail: The Longmont Housing Authority approved the tax exemption partnership on 2026-06-16 and the bond issuance on 2026-07-21, when staff said the project was on schedule to close financing and start construction on 2026-08-10. A preliminary official statement expected bond delivery in August 2026. No dated public record of the closing, a building permit or a groundbreaking was found.

next_step: Watch for a final official statement or EMMA filing for the Longmont Housing Authority Series 2026 bonds, a City of Longmont building permit, and a CHFA carryover or 8609 listing.

key_numbers.meaning: 18 one-bedroom and 54 two-bedroom units at 30% to 80% AMI; 38 of them at or below 50% AMI.
About $13.9M over 10 years, plus $1,733,276 of accelerated state credit and $14,250,000 of tax-exempt bonds.
The April 2026 budget given to City Council totals $31,825,936, including $2.12M for land and $18.17M for construction.

key_numbers.value: $1,742,842 city loan plus a 100% fee waiver
key_numbers.meaning: Council added $742,842 to a $1M 2023 loan and waived all eligible development fees to fill a $1,398,271 gap left by lost project-based vouchers.

facts.value: 130 Third Avenue, Longmont 80501 (northeast corner of E. 3rd Avenue and Atwood Street)
One four-story, L-shaped, wood-frame (Type VA) elevator building on spread footings, with surface and tuck-under parking. Average unit sizes 538 sq ft (1BR) and 720 sq ft (2BR)

About one acre in qualified census tract 134.01, zoned MU-D (Mixed Use Downtown). Sources give 1.06, 1.0036 and 0.9441 acres. Zoning is use-by-right. The site has existing structures over 50 years old
42 on-site resident spaces, plus street parking on Atwood Street and 3rd Avenue
OUR Center, about 380 feet away, provides on-site and nearby services (meals, food pantry, financial literacy, employment referrals) under an MOU
All-electric, 135 kW rooftop solar, NGBS Bronze target, two EV chargers
Bus stop about 260 feet away. RTD NECO passes budgeted for every household
7 Type A units and communication features in all units, per the city application; the narrative says 12.5% of units are designed for disabled households
Brikwell Olive Grove Housing Owner, LLC, managed by Brikwell Olive Grove Housing Solutions, LLC

Exempt through a Longmont Housing Authority partnership: LHA Ventures, LLC joins as a 0.01% special limited partner for up to 18 years for a $172,511 fee at closing plus a $3,000 annual asset management fee and a right of first refusal
Bond regulatory agreement: at least 40 years after 50% occupancy. City inclusionary agreement: permanent deed restriction with a buyout option after 30 years. See discrepancies

background.text: The project entered Longmont's development review on 2020-11-25. The purchase contract dates from March 2023, and the site is still held under a purchase and sale agreement; land is budgeted at $2,121,221.

In June 2023 the Longmont Housing Authority board, which is the City Council, took up a commitment to a property tax exemption partnership. Staff then estimated a 69% exemption worth about $935,000 over 15 years, because state law may not exempt the 70-80% AMI units.

Council took up a voluntary alternative agreement (R-2023-57) on 2023-06-20 to meet inclusionary housing rules with 38 units at or below 50% AMI. The term sheet calls for permanent affordability with a buyout option after 30 years. The city also approved a $1,000,000 Affordable Housing Fund loan on 2023-06-20.

Earlier versions of the deal included 20% AMI units with project-based vouchers. The 2024 Round Two application had 4 units at 20% AMI and 9 at 30% AMI. By 2025 all 13 deepest units were at 30% AMI, with 8 carrying vouchers.

The 2025 award was the project's third tax credit attempt. LHA staff wrote that CHFA cited the lack of private activity bonds as the main reason the fall 2024 application failed, so the developer obtained Longmont's full 2025 bond allocation of $6,415,747 (R-2025-33, 2025-06-17).

In February 2026, after talks with HUD, LHA said it could no longer provide the eight project-based vouchers its board had authorized on 2023-07-18, because doing so would put LHA in deficit. The lost rent ($109,824 a year) cut debt proceeds by $1,398,271.

Council approved a 100% fee waiver and an extra $742,842 from the Affordable Housing Fund on 2026-04-28, ahead of the normal June funding cycle, so the deal could close in July 2026. An independent council newsletter reported both votes as 6-1.

Once the deal won credits, CHFA agreed to supply more bond cap. Council then split the city's 2025 allocation, about $3,415,747 for Atwood Commons and $3,000,000 for Parkside & Mountain View Plaza (R-2026-33, on the 2026-06-09 agenda).
City staff report the 70% and 80% AMI units are underwritten at about 63% AMI rents. The 50 units at or below 60% AMI count toward Longmont's Prop 123 commitment.
The Phase I and II environmental reports found about 300 cubic yards of diesel- and oil-impacted soil to be removed under supervision.
The market study found 50% and 60% AMI penetration slightly above CHFA's preferred level, but surveyed LIHTC properties were 96% occupied.

discrepancies.text: CHFA's award report lists CHFA as bond issuer, and the 2025 application said CHFA would issue, while the Longmont Housing Authority resolution, the city's June 2026 council communication and the preliminary official statement name the Longmont Housing Authority as issuer.

The applicant and the 2026 city funding application say the site plan and plat were approved in May 2024, while the April 2026 council communication says the project received entitlements in late 2025.

The 2023 inclusionary term sheet calls for permanent affordability with a buyout option after 30 years, the April 2026 council communication says affordability in perpetuity, and the 2026 city funding application gives a 40-year affordability period.
The CHFA application and the 2026 city funding application name the Longmont Housing Authority as property manager, while the preliminary official statement names Yarco Company, Inc.
Total cost appears as $31,825,936 in the April 2026 budget given to Council, $30,942,766 in the 2026 city funding application, and $34,482,508 of total sources in the preliminary official statement.
CHFA's award description says the Longmont Housing Authority will provide eight project-based vouchers, while the April 2026 council communication says LHA withdrew them in February 2026.

The 2023 Longmont Leader article and LHA advisory memo describe 13 units at 20% AMI, while the 2023 council term sheet lists 13 units at or below 30% AMI (and its staff summary lists 4 at 20% and 9 at 30%).
LHA memos in 2025 and 2026 describe the project as serving 20% to 80% AMI, while CHFA, the city's 2026 council items and the preliminary official statement give 30% to 80% AMI.
